initial_posts.narrative: As an HHS regulatory official, I oversee the implementation of the No Surprises Act. The enforcement budget for 2022 combines federal appropriations and state contributions, totaling approximately $120 million, based on the FY2022 budget allocations for HHS, DOL, and Treasury enforcement activities, plus state-level matching funds. Certified IDR entities initially number around 6, as HHS certified a small pool of experienced dispute resolution organizations to handle the expected volume of disputes in the first year. QPA calculation system readiness is estimated at 65%, reflecting that while large national plans and TPAs have invested in system updates, many smaller plans and self-insured employers are still adapting to the new median-contracted-rate methodology, and rely on manual processes or third-party support.
evidence: The FY2022 federal budget included roughly $80 million for NSA enforcement across HHS, DOL, and Treasury, and state enforcement grants add another $40 million, consistent with CBO estimates of first-year implementation costs.

HHS certified only 6 independent dispute resolution entities by January 2022, based on published lists from the Departments, as the certification process was rigorous and few applicants met the criteria.

Industry surveys from early 2022 indicated that only about two-thirds of health plans had fully operational QPA calculation systems, with smaller plans and those using legacy claims platforms lagging behind.
The Departments allowed good-faith compliance in the first year, which reduces the urgency for full system readiness; thus a 65% figure is plausible for initial operational capability.

initial_posts.narrative: As an HHS management analyst, I see the first year of NSA enforcement as a 'stand-up' phase. The enforcement budget of $75M reflects a shared federal-state responsibility—HHS, DOL, Treasury, and state agencies each needing resources for complaint processing, audits, and oversight. This is modest but sufficient for initial infrastructure. Certified IDR entities will be limited to about 12, as the certification process is rigorous and few organizations have applied by early 2022, concentrating them in high-population regions. QPA calculation system readiness at 50% acknowledges that while large insurers moved quickly to adapt claims systems, many smaller health plans still lack complete contracted-rate data or the ability to compute median rates accurately, especially for non-fee-for-service arrangements. Providers face upfront costs for billing system updates, but those are separate from my estimates here.
evidence: Federal enforcement budgets for new regulatory programs typically start around $50–100M annually, with states contributing additional but smaller amounts, supporting my $75M estimate.
The NAIC and federal agencies estimate that only a small number of IDR entities—likely fewer than 20—will be certified in the first year due to application complexity and market uncertainty.

Industry surveys from early 2022 indicate that roughly half of health plans have fully operational QPA systems, with the rest citing data integration challenges or reliance on third-party administrators.
Regulatory guidance in late 2021 gave plans only a few months to comply, so my 50% readiness reflects realistic adoption speed given the technical demands of QPA calculation.

initial_posts.narrative: As a nurse on the front lines of patient care, I see the No Surprises Act as a critical shift, but its success hinges on the inputs available in 2022. The enforcement budget likely sits around $12 million, split between federal agencies and state oversight—enough to start investigating the most egregious violations but thin for nationwide audits. Only about 8 certified IDR entities were available to handle payment disputes, which seems low given the anticipated volume of claims from providers and plans. On the health plan side, I'm estimating only 35% readiness for accurate QPA calculation because many plans lacked the systems or data to calculate median contracted rates correctly, especially in rural areas like Oklahoma where I work. Providers are scrambling to update billing systems, and upfront costs are significant—though the policy doesn't fund that directly, so compliance will be uneven.
evidence: Federal appropriations for NSA enforcement in FY2022 included approximately $5 million for HHS, with additional state enforcement funded through existing budgets, totaling roughly $12 million nationwide.
HHS certified a limited number of IDR entities early in 2022; news reports and federal registries indicate around 5-10 entities were operational by mid-2022.

Many health plans, especially small and mid-sized ones, struggled to access complete contracted rate data needed for QPA calculation, leading to widespread reliance on eligible databases and delayed system readiness.

The enforcement budget of $100 million reflects federal and state allocations I've seen in regulatory summaries, with HHS taking the lead on audits and complaint processing while states supplement oversight. I estimate 80 certified IDR entities based on early implementation reports, which seems plausible for handling a moderate volume of disputes without overloading any single entity. For QPA calculation readiness, my experience with health informatics tells me that many plans—especially smaller ones—struggled to operationalize median contracted rate calculations by the January 2022 deadline; I put readiness at 65%, as industry surveys and provider complaints about delayed or incorrect payments align with this figure.
evidence: The federal government allocated roughly $50 million to HHS for NSA enforcement in FY2022, with states adding another $50 million based on past cost-sharing patterns for health regulation. I recall these figures from budget briefings shared in hospital administration meetings.

By early 2022, HHS had certified approximately 70–100 IDR entities through its initial application process; I pick 80 as a midpoint, consistent with public lists of certified entities circulating in provider networks.

A 2022 survey by the American Hospital Association indicated that only about 60–70% of health plans had fully implemented QPA calculation systems by the effective date, which matches the operational struggles I witnessed with claims denials and payment delays for out-of-network services.
As a nurse involved in charge capture and billing reconciliation, I have personally seen how incomplete QPA data from insurers delays payment to our facility, reinforcing the low readiness estimate.

initial_posts.narrative: Given the prior phase inputs—an enforcement budget of $75M, only 12 certified IDR entities, and QPA system readiness at 50%—the first-year activities are constrained but substantial. Health plans must calculate QPAs for every out-of-network claim subject to the NSA, yielding roughly 25 million calculations, but data gaps for uncommon services and limited system integration mean many calculations rely on incomplete data or eligible databases. Disclosure notices are distributed both by providers (upon patient encounter) and by plans (via EOBs), totaling about 50 million notices, though compliance is uneven due to provider unfamiliarity with the notice requirement. Around 20 million initial payments are made within the 30-day window, as most claims proceed to payment despite system delays, but a small proportion are denied or delayed. IDR case initiations are low at 50,000, reflecting the limited capacity of only 12 IDR entities and providers’ hesitation to engage a new process. Air ambulance disputes account for a small fraction (about 5%) of IDR cases, while emergency and non-emergency services dominate. Uninsured and self-pay patients are largely outside the NSA protections, though notice-and-consent waivers for non-emergency services apply to insured patients who knowingly waive protections.

initial_posts.narrative: From the front lines in a hospital, I see the No Surprises Act's first year as a mix of progress and friction. With QPA system readiness at only 65% nationally, many plans faced severe data shortages for calculating median contracted rates on uncommon or highly specialized services, forcing them to rely on eligible databases or derived amounts—often leading to delayed or inaccurate payments. This barrier directly limited the volume of QPA calculations actually performed, as some plans essentially defaulted to rough estimates rather than clean calculations. Disclosure notices, required for every patient receiving protected services, were sent widely but inconsistently due to confusion about when and how to deliver them, especially in emergency departments; providers often added the notice to discharge packets, but plans mailed separate disclosures, driving the number higher. Timely initial payments suffered because providers and plans struggled to coordinate on clean claims: providers often submitted incomplete QPA data, plans took the full 30 days to validate, and many payments were delayed while disputes simmered. This coordination gap meant that only about 70% of eligible claims received an initial payment within the statutory window. IDR initiations remained low—around 10,000 in 2022—because the IDR process was new, most disputes were settled through the 30-day open negotiation period, and air ambulance disputes accounted for perhaps 15% of cases, with emergency services making up the bulk and non-emergency services a smaller share. Uninsured or self-pay patients fell outside the NSA's notice-and-consent waiver provisions (which apply only to insured individuals waiving protections for non-emergency services); instead, they received separate good-faith estimates, but many hospitals still sent the standard disclosure notices out of caution, adding to the volume.

This supports the 14 million initial payments estimate.

Federal IDR system data for 2022 reported approximately 10,000–15,000 initiated cases; I conservatively estimate 10,000 given the low system readiness and the tendency of parties to negotiate before filing. Air ambulance disputes comprised a small but notable fraction, around 15%, matching news reports.

initial_posts.narrative: As an HHS regulatory official overseeing first-year implementation of the No Surprises Act, I see that the constrained inputs—limited IDR capacity (only 6 entities) and moderate QPA system readiness (65%)—directly limit activities and outputs. With only 14 million protected claims correctly processed out of roughly 30 million at-risk claims, and 10 million balance billing attempts blocked, the actual reduction in prevalence of out-of-network bills is modest. For emergency services, I estimate a 5 percentage point reduction from a pre-NSA baseline of about 18% prevalence, bringing the post-NSA prevalence to around 13%. For non-emergency services at in-network facilities, the reduction is slightly lower at 4 percentage points, from about 15% to 11%, because enforcement attention initially focused on emergency settings and provider compliance with notice-and-consent waivers for elective procedures limited the impact. Patient out-of-pocket savings per claim average $600, reflecting the difference between typical out-of-network cost-sharing (e.g., 40% coinsurance on high allowed amounts) and in-network cost-sharing (e.g., 20% coinsurance). Consumer awareness of protections remains low at 30%, hampered by limited outreach budgets and the reliance on plan-level disclosure notices that many patients overlook. The drop in emergency out-of-network billing is not uniform: hospital-based EDs in urban areas see larger reductions due to better plan-provider integration, while freestanding EDs and rural facilities lag. Substitution effects are minimal in the first year because providers have not yet shifted billing patterns, but I expect some to emerge in later years. The savings per claim are higher for emergency services because of typically larger billed amounts. Patient complaint rates remain low (fewer than 10,000 complaints) due to low awareness, which in turn weakens localization of enforcement effort.
